The claimed account publishes a gist, tweet, toot, Telegram message, Bluesky post or Discord message containing 'Verifying that I control the following Nostr public key: <npub>'.
Only the key holder (event signature) and the anchor platform (hosting the post) are involved. No issuer or attestor.
The user posts the proof by hand. The spec defines no OAuth step.
It is a claim of control ('I control this npub'), not a grant of authority.
The defined platforms are github, twitter, mastodon, telegram, bluesky and discord. DNS anchoring is a separate NIP (NIP-05).
No email platform is defined.
GitHub, Twitter/X, Mastodon, Telegram, Bluesky, Discord.
The proof is only a pointer (gist id, tweet id). The verifier must fetch the post from the platform to check that it contains the npub.
For example, fetch https://gist.github.com/<identity>/<proof>.
No issuer key is involved.
The kind 10011 event authenticates itself (Schnorr signature). It can come from any relay or be presented directly. Relays are transport, not an authority that must be queried.
Verification needs only the signed event and the anchor platform. Nostr has no central service run by the spec authors.
Proofs are posts on the platform. The PR states that Discord proofs cannot be checked by clients that are not in the server. X tweet fetching already depends on an API or scraping.
The proof text names one npub. Nostr has no merged key-rotation NIP (no 41.md on master), and NIP-26 delegation is marked unrecommended. A new key needs new proofs.
No revocation construct exists. The user can only publish a new replaceable kind 10011 without the tag, or delete the post.
No expiry is defined. The PR asks verifiers to accept old-format proofs indefinitely.
Key migration and recovery proposals (#158, #829, #1032, #1056, #1452) are all unmerged. No 41.md exists on master as of 2026-10-01.

Proof text has no nonce or date. The created_at of the event is not tied to the post date, and no log exists. Verification is a live fetch, so a proof left on a transferred account (e.g. a Mastodon instance domain changing hands) still verifies.
Kind 10011 is a replaceable event. Relays keep only the latest one, so there is no append-only history.
The user can run their own relay for the record. The proof itself lives on the anchor platform by design.
The survey in the PR collected kind 10011 from 11 major relays. Clients publish the same signed event to many independent relays.
The proof text names an npub (secp256k1 BIP-340 key), and the claim must be a signed Nostr event.
Platform names are open strings. The survey found Bluesky (271) and Discord (70) claims published before the spec defined them. Verifiers still need per-platform fetch logic.
Community NIP, labeled 'draft optional'.
Two substantive changes in 2026: moved to kind 10011 (2026-02-10, #2216), and unified text plus Bluesky and Discord (2026-09-27, #2486).

A plain static file on a domain the user can control, with no platform API. For names hosted by a provider (e.g. primal.net), verification depends on that provider continuing to serve the file.

The mapping names one hex key. The domain owner can re-point the name to a new key without the old key, which is the de facto Nostr 'migration'. But the spec says clients follow pubkeys, not identifiers, so follows do not move.
Removing or changing the nostr.json entry is the only path. Clients 'should cease displaying' the identifier when the domain stops confirming it.
No expiry. Clients cache at their own discretion, e.g. Brainstorm-UI caches 30 min (https://github.com/NosFabrica/Brainstorm-UI/pull/87).
Nostr has no merged recovery NIP. NIP-05 lets a name be re-pointed, but the old pubkey's followers and history are not migrated.
No timestamps, nonces or log. Verification is a live fetch, so a new domain owner fully controls the result. An old proof cannot be replayed, but the new owner can re-bind the name.
Neither kind 0 (replaceable) nor nostr.json keeps history.
The user can host nostr.json on their own domain and the kind 0 on their own relay. A registrar is still needed for the domain.
The kind 0 record replicates across independent relays. The nostr.json proof is on a single web host.

For did:plc (the deployed default) the at://handle entry in alsoKnownAs is part of a PLC operation signed by a rotation key. For did:web the DID doc is a plain HTTPS file and is not signed.
The domain publishes the DID in DNS TXT _atproto.<handle> (did=...) or at https://<handle>/.well-known/atproto-did.
The PLC directory validates and orders operations but does not sign them; only rotation keys sign. No third-party attestation is involved.
The link is made by editing DNS or a well-known file and updating the DID doc. No OAuth login to the domain is involved.
This is a two-way claim of sameness (DID doc names the handle, domain names the DID). It does not delegate authority.
The handle is a DNS name, resolved via DNS TXT or HTTPS well-known.
The only handle form is a DNS hostname. Email addresses are not handles.
Only domains are supported. A platform can act as an anchor only by giving out subdomains (as bsky.social does).
The spec requires live resolution of both handle to DID and DID to doc, and says handles must not be trusted until the DID doc is confirmed to link back.
The verifier must query DNS or fetch https://<handle>/.well-known/atproto-did.
There is no issuer. PLC operations are self-certifying through rotation-key signatures.
did:plc (the deployed default) must be resolved via the PLC directory or a replica. did:web avoids the registry but is a minority path.

did:plc can be resolved from community mirrors or self-run validating replicas (open source, go-didplc), and did:web needs no Bluesky service at all. In practice most clients use plc.directory, which Bluesky PBC still runs.
The anchor is DNS or HTTPS on the user's own domain, so there is no platform API to close.
The handle binds to the DID, not to a key. Rotation and signing keys can change through PLC operations without breaking the DNS record.
A signed PLC operation can remove or replace alsoKnownAs, which ends the bidirectional link. Removing the DNS TXT also works.
Handles do not expire by design. The spec only recommends periodic re-resolution of cached results.
Rotation keys are listed in priority order (1-5 keys). A higher-priority key can override operations by lower keys within 72 hours.

Verification is a live two-way check. If the domain changes hands and the new owner repoints DNS, the old DID's claim fails and is shown as handle.invalid. PLC operations are also hash-chained with timestamps.

PLC keeps a public audit log (/log/audit, /export), but it is not yet a Merkle transparency log, and the directory can drop accepted operations. A Sunlight-style tlog is planned (sequence numbers were added in Jan 2026).
With did:web plus your own domain, both the record and the proof are self-hosted. did:web gets no migration or recovery support, and did:plc cannot be self-hosted.
Only one authoritative PLC directory accepts writes. Mirrors and replicas are read-only copies, and in Sept 2025 only about 3 public mirrors existed.
Only did:plc and did:web are supported, and keys must be secp256k1 or P-256. Ed25519 and other DID methods are not accepted.
The only anchor type is a DNS hostname. Any other anchor would need a spec change.

An IETF ATP WG was chartered in March 2026, and its scope covers identifier resolution requirements and a registry of methods such as PLC and did:web. The handle and did:plc specs are still published by Bluesky and PLC, not as adopted drafts.
PLC read replicas (Feb 2026), export API changes (Jan 2026), and the PLC Org setup (Sept 2026).

You must create an atproto identity (DID doc with #atproto key and at:// alsoKnownAs).
The record lives in the verifier's repo. The subject's key never signs anything.
No external anchor publishes anything. The verifier's record names the subject DID, handle, and displayName.
The verifier (Bluesky or a trusted-verifier org) writes the record into its own repo, and that repo commit is signed by the verifier's atproto signing key.
Verification is an editorial decision by Bluesky moderation or a trusted verifier org. No OAuth to an external account is involved.
The record is an attestation about a subject DID, not a delegation. Trusted-verifier status works like a CA hierarchy, but it is configured in the AppView rather than expressed as a capability.

The record snapshots the handle string, which may be a domain, but it attests to off-protocol authenticity and notability, not control of a domain. Bluesky says domain handles are 'different from a verification badge'.
The record has no email field.
The record has no field for an external account. It attests that the atproto account belongs to an authentic or notable entity.
Validity requires the issuer to be trusted by the app and the current handle and displayName to match the record. Both need live state, and in the Bluesky app the AppView computes them.
There is no external anchor to fetch. The verifier reads the issuer repo or the AppView.
Per the lexicon, verifications are valid only if issued by an account the app considers trusted.
Issuer and subject DIDs (mostly did:plc) must be resolved to check signatures and current handles.

In practice validity (verifiedStatus, trustedVerifierStatus, isValid) is computed by the Bluesky AppView. The root issuer bsky.app and its records are on Bluesky infrastructure, and the trusted-verifier list is set by Bluesky.
There is no external anchor platform. Issuer records stay readable from PDS and relays even without Bluesky's AppView, though a client would need its own verifier list.
The record names the subject DID, not a key, so key rotation does not affect it. Changing the handle or displayName does invalidate it.

Besides deleting the record, the AppView can mark a trusted verifier invalid (trustedVerifierStatus), which voids all of its verifications. Handle or displayName changes also invalidate automatically.
Only createdAt is stored. There is no expiry field.
Inherited from did:plc rotation keys for the subject and issuer accounts. The verification feature itself defines no recovery.
The record binds a DID plus a snapshot of the handle and displayName, and is valid only while both still match. The record is mutable and can be deleted live.
Repos are mutable signed Merkle trees. Records can be deleted with no tombstone, and there is no append-only log.
The proof must be issued by Bluesky or a Bluesky-approved trusted verifier from that verifier's repo. A user cannot self-issue a recognized check.
Records are relayed over the firehose, but recognized validity comes from one operator, the Bluesky AppView. Other networks such as Eurosky/mu run separate verifier sets.
The subject must be an atproto DID.
No external anchors are defined. New trusted verifiers can be added without a spec change, but those are issuers, not anchors.
This is a vendor lexicon (app.bsky.*), and the IETF ATP charter excludes app-specific schemas and the moderation system.
In 2026 Eurosky/mu reuses app.bsky.graph.verification with its own verifiers, and other apps (Sifa) are adding attributed display.

The X/GitHub link is a UserDataAdd (TWITTER=8, GITHUB=9) message signed by an ed25519 app key registered to the user's fid. That key is held by the Farcaster app, not by the user. For ETH/SOL verifications, the fid's signer signs a VerificationAddAddress naming the address.

X and GitHub publish nothing naming the fid. The only bidirectional case is ETH/Solana address verification, where the address signs an EIP-712 claim naming the fid. Those addresses are not social or DNS anchors.
FIP-19: the attesting app (Warpcast, now the Farcaster app run by Neynar) signs the X/GitHub binding after OAuth. Verifiers must choose which attesting fids to trust.

The anchor link is a sameness attestation. Capability delegation exists only inside Farcaster: custody address authorizes app signer keys in KeyRegistry.
There is no DNS-domain verification type. Username proofs cover only fnames and ENS (.eth) names, and the URL user-data field is unverified.
No email user-data or verification type exists in the protocol messages.

No external anchor is involved. The public key itself is the TLD.
Packets are self-signed by the ed25519 key, and relays only verify and forward them.
Publishing is an unauthenticated DHT put or relay PUT of a self-signed packet.
No delegation semantics. The packet holds DNS resource records.
The inverse holds: the key becomes a DNS-like TLD. No ICANN domain is anchored to the key or verified. ICANN domains appear only as HTTPS endpoint targets.

Not required to check a presented packet. Discovering the record or its freshness means a Mainline DHT (or relay) lookup.
Resolution goes directly over the Mainline DHT (BEP44). Synonym-run relays are optional and needed only in UDP-less environments such as browsers.
No anchor platform API is involved.
The public key is the name, and the spec defines no rotation or succession. A new key is a new identity.
The only option is to publish a newer packet (higher timestamp) that overwrites records. There is no revocation or tombstone mechanism.
README: records are ephemeral, the DHT drops them after hours, so republish periodically. Records also carry DNS TTLs.
No recovery is defined. Losing the ed25519 secret key means losing the name.
The signed microsecond timestamp acts as the BEP44 seq, and older packets are rejected (relay 409). Caveat: anyone can republish an old signed packet if the DHT has forgotten the newer one.
The DHT keeps only the latest mutable item, with no history.
The user's own client can put directly to Mainline DHT with no operator account.
Mainline DHT has about 10M nodes, and records are stored on several nodes near sha1(pubkey).
Only ed25519 keys work, and the key is its own identifier. It does not anchor other keys or DIDs, though did:dht (DIF) layers a DID document on top as TXT records.
There is no anchor concept. Arbitrary TXT records could carry claims, but nothing defines or verifies them.
